blind_target.authors: Hulleman, C. S., Godes, O., Hendricks, B. L., & Harackiewicz, J. M.
blind_target.title: Enhancing interest and performance with a utility value intervention.
blind_target.evidence_quote: Although the research generated by the expectancy-value framework has been largely correlational (Wigfield & Cambria, 2010), recent classroom studies reveal that interventions designed to enhance perceptions of value can increase both interest and course perfor- mance (e.g., Hulleman & Harackiewicz, 2009; Hulleman, Godes, Hendricks, & Harackiewicz, 2010). The research presented herein replicates and extends this prior work by further investigating a theory-based intervention designed to enhance student motivation and performance.
blind_target.outcome_quote: The results of Study 2 partially replicated prior research dem- onstrating that a theoretically guided intervention based on the expectancy-value framework could enhance student learning out- comes (Hulleman & Harackiewicz, 2009; Hulleman et al., 2010).
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors explicitly give a partial-replication verdict over both cited prior intervention papers; interest/performance benefits coexist with an unexpected mechanism.

prior_decision.quote: The utility value interventions utilized in the current studies were based on the self-generated utility value interventions used by Hulleman and colleagues (e.g., Hulleman et al., 2010; Hulleman & Harackiewicz, 2009). In addition to replicating this prior research, we extend it in five ways.
prior_decision.reason: Omitted target: Hulleman et al. (2010) (DOI: 10.1037/a0019506) is an independent original paper explicitly cited throughout the introduction, methods, and discussion alongside Hulleman & Harackiewicz (2009) as prior utility value intervention research replicated in Study 2, and shares the same 'mixed' partial-replication verdict in the Study 2 Discussion.

blind_target.evidence_quote: The main aim of the study was to replicate and extend van Prooijen's findings on how education and its outcomes (cognitive complexity, subjective social standing, self‐esteem, a feeling of control and powerlessness, cognitive reflection, epistemic curiosity and scientific reasoning) predict conspiracy beliefs.

blind_target.title: Differential behavioral effects of gonadal steroids in women with and in those without premenstrual syndrome.
blind_target.evidence_quote: We evaluated differences between cohorts, attempted to replicate our original findings of a differential behavioral sensitivity to otherwise similar changes in ovarian steroids in women with PMDD compared to healthy comparison women (3), and examined several as yet unanswered questions about the effects of ovarian steroids on symptoms in these women.
blind_target.outcome_quote: This confirms and replicates our original finding that women with PMDD and healthy comparison women who do not have PMDD have different behavioral responses to the same physiological exposures to both estradiol and progesterone, a phenomenon that, in this experimental paradigm, distinguishes women with PMDD from women without.

shipped_originals.title_o: Children's acquisition of the number words and the counting system

blind_target.title: Children's understanding of counting
blind_target.evidence_quote: The present work focused on the GaN from Wynn's (1990Wynn's ( , 1992) ) studies with no intention to test the replicability of results coming from the other tasks (i.e., the Point-to-x task or the colour control task were not administered).
blind_target.outcome_quote: Supporting this view, Large-numbers knowers (4-to 7-knowers) were found to be more likely to resort to counting for large number words than for small ones in study 1. In addition, several children switched from a grabbing to a counting strategy around four. However, the majority of participants kept a consistent strategy all along the task and many of them still succeeded at giving large numbers with a grabbing strategy. Thus, the strategy, at least as coded here, could not be considered as what makes the difference to acquire the cardinal knowledge of large number words.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The authors explicitly report agreement with some original observations and disagreement with others; no overall replication verdict supersedes those comparisons.

prior_decision.quote: The present work focused on the GaN from Wynn's (1990Wynn's ( , 1992) ) studies with no intention to test the replicability of results coming from the other tasks (i.e., the Point-to-x task or the colour control task were not administered).
prior_decision.reason: Omitted target. The authors explicitly frame their work as a conceptual replication of the Give-a-Number (GaN) observations from both Wynn (1990) and Wynn (1992), and in Study 1 they directly re-test Wynn's (1990) counter vs. grabber strategy predictions (line 30) as well as the all-at-once generalization assumption attributed to Wynn (1990, 1992) (line 28), finding mixed support (confirming that large-number knowers count more frequently for large than small numbers, but finding sequential acquisition of large number words and no difference between terminal-counters and terminal-grabbers in reaching large-number knowledge).
